texts.orig: The present work aims to provide a complete engineering solution, an appropriate experimental database, and a brief physical background on designing a miniature specimen geometry suitable for irradiation in materials test reactors such as the High Flux Isotope Reactor and post-irradiation out-of-hot cell testing. The physical limits of specimen miniaturization and a background of the scale factor effect are discussed, and principal limitations are defined. The advantages of modern test methods like digital image correlation, as well as some limitations connected to small specimen size, are analyzed. A subsized specimen geometry, ''SS-Mini,' is designed; the geometry employs existing irradiation capsules leading to the reduced cost of any irradiation campaign. The new geometry performance is evaluated using a commercial 304 L stainless steel, an aluminum alloy including advanced 3D-printed material, a high nickel 718-alloy, tungsten, and an advanced fuel cladding FeCrAl alloy. Mechanical tests are conducted to compare the engineering mechanical properties (yield and ultimate tensile stress, uniform and total elongation values) and plastic behavior of the proposed miniature specimen with common specimen types for irradiation testing.

texts.orig: Irradiation may stimulate specific processes not observed without irradiation, including swelling, increased diffusion and creep, radiation-induced segregation (RIS), and irradiation-assisted stress corrosion cracking (IASCC), just to name a few. Advanced in-situ tools may bring new insights into well-known processes. For instance, a preliminary, not-on-purpose analysis of the deformation localization in neutron irradiated austenitic steels revealed specific phase transformation at the irradiated specimen's surface (Gussev et al., 2014b) along with areas of localized deformation and high dislocation density spots (Field et al. 2014a) in addition to the expected and well-known defect-free channels. It is important to be able to test the irradiated specimen in-situ, registering, for example, the evolution of dislocation density and the evolution of local misorientation (Jiang et al., 2013) with direct measurements of acting stress or observations of stress corrosion crack appearance and propagation. These data, coupled with modern modeling tools, allow for complex analysis of material behavior, including constitutive crystal plasticity approaches. However, to reach these goals, one has to at least have direct access to the specimen for preparing the appropriate quality surface.

texts.orig: Miniature sub-size specimens for post-radiation testing have a long history and are widely used for investigating mechanical properties and deformation-hardening behavior of irradiated and non-irradiated metals and alloys (Klueh, 1985; Panayotou et al., 1986; Kohyama et al., 1991; Kohno et al., 2000; Gussev et al., 2014a), weldments (Field et al., 2014b), nanostructured materials, and different composites. A variety of different sizes and geometries are used in nuclear materials science (Klueh, 1985; Pierron et al., 2003; Wakai et al., 2011), with new geometries and testing methods being constantly developed (Rickerby and Fenici, 1986; Dz ˇugan et al., 2014; Hurst and Matocha, 2015; Rund et al., 2015). Specimen miniaturization often involved other methods, not only tensile testing. Thus, Jung et al., (1996) offered a miniature tensile specimen with gauge section of 5 -1 -0.4 mm; additionally, a number of testing methods for miniature specimens (tensile, facture toughness, punching, impact testing) were discussed in detail (Jung et al., 1996) focusing on the detailed correlation between miniature and bulk behavior. The offered tensile specimen geometry was intensively used in a number of projects (see for instance, (Dai and Bauer, 2001)).

texts.orig: The scale factor and size effects usually become apparent when the specimen size approaches the characteristic length scale of the material microstructure (Connolley et al., 2005). For common steels and alloys, this tends to be the grain size. Another size effect, often observed in brittle materials (Baz ˇant, 1999), occurs when the size of the specimen becomes small compared to the spatial distribution and density of critical defects. Additionally, size effects may appear due to physical, chemical, or corrosion processes that are negligible for relatively large objects but become critical when the size of the test specimen decreases. Most of these processes, like oxidation, usually do not appear in common mechanical tests; however, some important physical phenomena sensitive to the scale factor are briefly analyzed below.

texts.orig: In the first case, under uniaxial stress, the specimen is often presented as a ''multilayer' object with a layer of near-surface grains. The ratio of the ''near-surface grains' to the ''bulk grains' impacts the specimen deformation behavior and strain hardening rate (Wang et al., 2013; Shin et al., 2015). The near-surface grains (or the near-surface layer if a single crystal specimen is considered) have smaller dislocation density and internal back stress level compared to the bulk grains (Keller et al., 2010; Shin et al., 2015) because of the dislocation escape through the free surface. Also, the surface plays a key role in crack initiation during fatigue (Signor et al., 2016) and stress corrosion cracking (SCC). To handle very thin specimens (10-20 l msheets), some special test method (s) may be needed. For instance, Hoffman and Hong (Hoffmann and Hong, 2006) offered an aero-bulging test method for testing thin foils of different materials.

texts.orig: It is worth noting that the near-surface layer is not necessarily ''weak;' that is to say, it does not necessarily have a decreased strength. Often, specimens are produced by electric discharge machining (EDM) followed by mechanical grinding or polishing to fit the dimensional requirements. EDM leads to the formation of a recast surface layer, often referred to as the ''white layer' (Bleys et al., 2006), which may be hard and brittle depending on the material system. The subsequent mechanical grinding removes the EDM layer but introduces cold-work related artifacts or even results in the formation of fine grains (Kaneda et al., 2011). Electropolishing or controlled chemical etching may eliminate the modified layer, but these techniques are both costly and timeconsuming or produce specimens with thickness and edge shape variations that can significantly skew results.

texts.orig: Strictly speaking, it is impossible to avoid the free surface influence. Instead, the question is how thick should the specimen be to provide acceptable data? Usually, in mechanical test practice, the smallest specimen dimension should exceed 5-6 grains to minimize the scale factor influence (Kohno et al., 2000). This rule may not be fully valid in some specific cases (e.g., in nano-structured materials with high defect density). If defect spacing is much smaller than grain size, the bulk mechanical properties may be measured by using smaller specimens that contain as little as 2-4 grains across the smallest dimension (Howard et al., 2016).

texts.orig: Sometimes, there are additional limitations if the material being tested exhibits phenomena sensitive to the active volume or surface conditions. For instance, plastic deformation generates energy release in the form of heat and leads to a temperature increase (Ayres, 1985), but this process is usually ignored. However, the temperature at the specimen gauge may rise by 10 ° C or more even at a moderate strain rate (  10 � 3 s � 1 ) (Ayres, 1985). In the case of fracture, a large amount of energy is being released in a small volume resulting in a temperature jump that can reach 100 ° C. For example, a temperature rise of  300 ° C was observed in the shear bands in metallic glass specimens (Yang et al., 2006). As an ultimate case, melting of a metallic glass specimen during fracture was observed in-situ (Yang et al., 2004). In the tensile test, the heat generation is proportional to the specimen volume (  d 3 ) in the uniform strain area, whereas the heat losses rely on the specimen surface or cross-sectional area (  d 2 ). Thus, the heating intensity is proportional to the specimen size (d), being less pronounced in small specimens compared to larger ones. If the material of interest experiences strain-induced phase instability (Chen et al., 2013; Shirdel et al., 2015), such as the transformation induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, deformation twinning, or dynamic deformation aging, the effects of strain-induced heating should not be ignored.

In addition to the free surface effects and the different behavior of the near-surface grains, the neck also experiences a complex stress state. The neck shape and principal strain ratio may depend on specimen thickness and thickness-to-width ratio (T/W). Byun et al. (Byun et al., 1998) investigated the effect of specimen thickness on the mechanical properties of miniature specimens with a particular focus on deformation localization and necking. Regarding the yield and ultimate stress and uniform ductility for ferritic steels, Byun et al. concluded (Byun et al., 1998) that these values will be close to the bulk material data of the specimen if thickness exceeds  0.3-0.4 mm (or  7-10 -grain size).

texts.label: text
texts.orig: However, the total elongation value demonstrated a more complex behavior, as shown in Fig. 1, where saturation in the total elongation values was reached at  2 mm thickness (T/W ratio of  0.67 in Fig. 1). Necking angle, the angle between the loading axis and the fracture plane, was also affected by thickness. The parameter controlling these processes was found to be the T/W ratio that influences the stress state in the neck (Byun et al., 1998). A similar result-post-necking elongation increased with thickness-was obtained by (Yuan et al., 2012). In the context of the present work, this means that the T/W value of the conventional small-scale specimens, like SS-3 [T/W  0.5, (Klueh, 1985)], and new miniature geometries discussed later should be close, if not identical.

Thus, it is important to cover a wide range of strength and ductility values and different types of strain hardening behavior by using a vast array of different material systems. The present work included both well-known and advanced modern materials, as shown in Table 1. Aluminum 6061 alloy is employed to cover the low strength/low ductility range; also, after annealing, this material demonstrates specific deformation behavior with propagating deformation bands. Austenitic AISI 304L stainless steel is selected as a representative commercial, widely used nuclear material.

texts.orig: 1. The miniature specimen geometry should reproduce a polycrystalline-like behavior. To achieve this, the specimen should contain at least 5-6 (or more) grains per the smallest dimension. Generally, if the thinnest area has less than 5 grains, the specimen will demonstrate reduced strength. The most common grain size for ferrous and non-ferrous alloys is near 40-50 l m, resulting in  300-400 l m being the limiting minimal thickness for the specimen.

Fig. 5 shows plastic strain distribution obtained by DIC analysis in 304L steel specimens deformed at the overall strain level of  0.4. As shown in the data, the strain level reaches about half of the overall strain level (  0.2) observed at the gauge-head transition location (point A), and this value ( e A) is close for all specimen geometries. At the distance of  0.8 mm from this location (point B), the strain level ( e B) is still significant in the S-type specimen with reduced head size, whereas it drops to  0.03 in the E-type and SS-J specimen. Note that even the SS-J specimen, with relatively massive heads (in relation to the miniature specimens under investigation), is not large enough to completely eliminate plastic deformation in the heads. As distance from the gauge increases, local strain decreases quickly (see point C for SS-J specimen in Fig. 5). For the widest head portion, E- and SS-J geometries can provide virtually non-deformed material. Note also that plastic strain in the heads should reduce quickly with strength level increase.

If an irradiation project considers a new specimen geometry, it may be advantageous to maintain compatibility with existing infrastructure. To perform specimen irradiation at HFIR, which is an 85 MWt beryllium-reflected, pressurized, light-water-cooled and moderated flux-trap-type reactor (Xoubi and Primm III, 2005), small cylindrical ''rabbit' capsules were developed over two decades ago to take advantage of the very high neutron flux in this reactor (>10 15 n/cm 2 s in both the thermal and fast regions of the spectrum). Each of these capsules accommodated up to 24 SS-J type specimens. The general internal capsule design remains the same from project to project, with only the gas gap value being adjusted to meet projectspecific requirements for the irradiation temperature.

texts.orig: A key component of any irradiation program is to obtain the desired irradiation dose (in dpa and/or neutron fluence) and irradiation temperature. To address the newly developed SS-2E geometry impact on design temperatures, an ANSYS finite element analysis (FEA) model is used. Given the modular nature of the design, only a single tensile configuration layer located at the capsule centerline is analyzed to determine thermal performance. Scoping analyses are performed to show that all generic configurations of SS-J2/SS-2E tensile specimens perform in the same fashion, given the virtually identical heat loading and contact gaps seen in the loading permutations. Table 5 outlines this thermal equivalency for an irradiation running at a nominal temperature of 550 ° C. There is a larger span of temperatures for the SS-J specimen caused by the large temperature gradients observed in the grip section of the specimens. However, the tensile gauge lengths for the specimens are more analogous, as seen in Fig. 9. Hence, the SS2E specimen geometry and the pre-existing capsule design may be used in all flux trap positions available in the HFIR. Furthermore, the modular subassemblies provide inherent specimen grouping and simplify the post-irradiation disassembly. This feature provides valuable cost savings, given the relatively high cost of hot cell facility usage.

texts.text: 6. Conclusions

texts.label: text
texts.orig: The present work provides a complete engineering solution and experimental database on a small specimen geometry suitable for irradiation in materials test reactors and post-irradiation out-ofhot cell testing. A sub-sized specimen geometry, ''SS-Mini,' was designed; the new geometry leverages existing geometries, and configurations for irradiation capsules lead to reduced cost for deployment. The performance of the proposed geometry was evaluated using 304L stainless steel and several commercial alloys with several different strength and ductility levels. Mechanical tensile tests were carried out to compare the engineering mechanical properties (yield stress, ultimate tensile stress, and uniform and total elongation values) and plastic behavior of different miniature specimens. It is shown that the proposed specimen geometry provides acceptable mechanical property results and meets the design parameters for use in a materials test reactor.
